title: Sold for a few coins
hook: a caravan pulls him out and sells him cheaply in Egypt
carry: the price they paid isn't your worth

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabr jamil, and a father who named the lie and then waited. Your line was beautiful patience.

A caravan of travelers comes by the well. They send their water-drawer, and he lets down his bucket. It comes up heavy. He looks in and shouts: good news! Here's a boy! For a boy who's been waiting in the dark, that sounds like rescue. Except the men up top aren't rescuers. They're traders. And a boy, to a trader, is something else.
screen: `A CARAVAN COMES BY.` → `THE BUCKET COMES UP HEAVY.` → `GOOD NEWS! A BOY!`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. They hid him away as merchandise, and sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, counted out. The Arabic for that price is bakhs, a cheated, short-changed price, less than a thing is worth. And the verse adds: they thought little of him. The boy who dreamed the stars bowing, sold for pocket change by men who didn't much care. Commentators have noted that a price you can count, a few coins rather than a weighed amount, was itself a sign of how cheap it was. Now watch the next verse, because the Qur'an turns the whole scene around. The man in Egypt who bought him says to his wife: make his stay honorable. Perhaps he'll be of use to us, or we might take him as a son. Sound familiar? It should. Two weeks ago, in Pharaoh's palace, Pharaoh's wife, the woman tradition calls Asiya, looked at baby Musa and said almost the same words. Two boys, in two stories, taken into an Egyptian house by someone who saw what the world had missed. Then the verse says: and so We established Yusuf in the land, and Allah is in full command of His affairs, but most people don't know. The traders set the price. They didn't set his worth. The boy they sold for a handful of coins is, in the story's own words, being established. Nobody watching that sale could have guessed it.
screen: `HIDDEN AS MERCHANDISE.` · `BAKHS — A SHORT-CHANGED PRICE.` · `MAKE HIS STAY HONORABLE.` · `ESTABLISHED IN THE LAND.` · then, large: `THE PRICE ISN'T THE WORTH.`

segments.voice: Think of a time someone set a low price on you: passed over for the job, talked over in the meeting, treated like you were extra in your own family. Then gently separate two things, what they paid or thought or offered, and what you actually are, and say it to yourself slowly: that was their price, not my worth. If you pray, you can remember how the verse ends: Allah is in full command of His affairs.
Bakhs, a cheated price: what the traders paid for Yusuf, thinking little of him, while Allah was establishing him in the land.
Your line: the price they paid isn't your worth. The buyer in Egypt saw what the traders missed. Fifty-nine, and counting.

screen: `DAY 59 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HOUSE OF THE AZIZ.`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers draw from Yusuf's sale the lesson that human judgments of worth are not Allah's, and point to 12:21, which says Allah is in full command of His affairs, though most people don't know it.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:20: a paltry, short-changed price — less than the thing is worth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yusuf was unlucky.
what it means: traders set a low price on him, but the next verse says Allah was establishing him in the land.
what a scholar hears: 12:20's darahima ma'duda, coins counted out, suggests a sum small enough to count; 12:21 echoes the words of Pharaoh's wife over Musa in 28:9.
recall: a helper who shares the load

notes: 'Coins counted rather than weighed' as a sign of a small sum: a common tafsir explanation; confirm.
The parallel between 12:21 and 28:9 ('perhaps he will benefit us, or we will take him as a son') is exact in the Arabic ('asa an yanfa'ana aw nattakhidhahu waladan); confirm.
Who sold him (the caravan, or the brothers returning to claim him, as some commentators say) is discussed in tafsir; the script follows the plain sense (the caravan).
